title: Hemoglobin structure and function
covers: The red cell and its metabolism, the structure of hemoglobin and its heme pocket, the adult hemoglobins, T and R states with cooperative oxygen binding, the dissociation curve and P50, the four negative regulators, CO2 carriage with the Bohr and Haldane effects, and the biochemistry of carbon monoxide, thalassemia and sickle cell disease.

summary.h: The red cell and its metabolism

ul: Blood cells are erythrocytes, leukocytes and thrombocytes, all from hematopoietic stem cells in the marrow. Low tissue oxygen makes the kidney release erythropoietin, which drives red cell production.

A red cell is a flexible biconcave disk, 6–8 microns across and 2 microns thick. Its three jobs: carry oxygen from lungs to tissues, buffer the blood by binding protons, and so allow CO2 to travel as bicarbonate.
With no internal organelles its metabolism is limited, and glycolysis is the main energy pathway. Lactate production regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running.

table: Reduces methemoglobin (Fe³⁺) back to the ferrous state
The major allosteric effector of oxygen binding
Regenerates reduced glutathione, protecting membrane lipids and proteins from oxidation

items.caption: Red cell pathways: glycolysis with its two shunts

ul: About 270 million hemoglobin molecules per red cell, carrying around 98% of the oxygen in blood. At that concentration solubility depends on side-chain placement: hydrophobic residues buried in the core, hydrophilic residues on the water-exposed surface.
One molecule = 4 heme groups (iron + porphyrin ring) + 4 globin chains. Heme sits in a hydrophobic pocket, its iron coordinated to the proximal histidine, and is not covalently linked to the globin.
Each heme reversibly binds one O2, so the tetramer carries four.
The globin genes are switched on chronologically through development.

table: α chains 141 amino acids, non-α chains 146
Tetramer of two heterodimers, with allosteric interactions
Higher O2 affinity: it binds 2,3-BPG weakly
Plasma glucose over the last 2–3 months; 6.5% or more is diagnostic for diabetes

ul: Hemoglobin handles three diffusible ligands: O2 (delivery), CO2 (elimination) and NO (vascular tone).

summary.h: Binding oxygen: T, R and cooperativity

ul: The iron stays ferrous throughout: hemoglobin carries oxygen without oxidizing its heme. Oxyhemoglobin is the bound form, deoxyhemoglobin the unbound one.
In the lungs O2 binds, the inter-dimer bonds break, the dimers rotate on each other and hemoglobin shifts to R. In the tissues O2 is released and it returns to T.
Cooperativity: once the first O2 binds, the remaining hemes bind faster. That communication between the four hemes is heme-heme interaction, and it makes the curve sigmoid.

Pulse oximetry uses red light (about 660 nm) and infrared (about 940 nm). Oxyhemoglobin lets red light through and absorbs more infrared, so arterial blood looks bright red; deoxyhemoglobin absorbs more red, so venous blood looks darker.
About 98% saturation in the lungs at an arterial pO2 of 95 mmHg; 75% in peripheral tissues at a pO2 of 40 mmHg, so 25% of the load is delivered at rest.
The plateau between 70 and 100 mmHg is a safety margin: a fall from 100 to 50 mmHg costs only about 15% of saturation.
P50 is the pO2 at which hemoglobin is half-saturated, so it is a direct expression of affinity.

items.p: CO2, H+, Cl⁻ and 2,3-BPG all lower hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.

table: Binds the central cavity between the two β chains, stabilizing T and promoting delivery to tissues. In the lungs the pO2 is high enough to load O2 anyway. Without BPG, hemoglobin loads oxygen more readily
Stabilizes T by strengthening the inter-subunit bonds and 2,3-BPG binding — the Bohr effect
Binds the N terminus of the globins as carbaminohemoglobin, stabilizing T

ul: HbF binds 2,3-BPG weakly, which is why it holds oxygen more tightly than HbA.

summary.h: Carrying CO2, and the Bohr and Haldane effects

table: Form of CO2 leaving the tissues
Bicarbonate, after carbonic anhydrase hydrates CO2

ul: Inside the red cell the H+ is buffered by hemoglobin and phosphate; the bicarbonate leaves to buffer the blood against other metabolic acids.
Chloride shift: bicarbonate leaving the cell in the tissues is matched by Cl⁻ entering, keeping the charge balanced.
At the lungs the whole equilibrium reverses: CO2 is released, H+ recombines with bicarbonate, and hemoglobin loses H+ so it binds oxygen more readily.
Bohr effect: H+ (and CO2) lower O2 affinity by stabilizing T. Haldane effect: oxygen binding in the lungs shifts hemoglobin to R, releasing H+ and CO2 and helping CO2 unloading.

table: Right shift (Bohr); CO2 and H+ bind the globin portion and alter its conformation
Right shift; rises with chronic hypoxia — altitude, smoking, COPD
The more active the tissue, the higher its pCO2, H+ and temperature, so more O2 is released at the same pO2

ul: The logic of altitude: lower pO2 means less saturation leaving the lungs, so BPG rises to squeeze more oxygen out in the tissues.

Carbon monoxide: colorless, odorless, can be fatal. It binds the oxygen sites 200–250 times more strongly than O2, so it outcompetes oxygen, and its conformational effect shifts the curve left, so what is still carried is released less readily.

items.note: Slide 36 calls CO's affinity "several orders of magnitude" higher and then gives 200–250 times. Only the 200–250 figure was tested.

ul: Erythropoietin doping: more circulating red cells means thicker blood and thrombosis risk, with better aerobic capacity. EPO also drives cell-survival pathways through its receptor, so it may promote cancer; in cancer patients EPO-like drugs shortened survival or sped tumor growth, and have carried an FDA boxed warning since 2007.

table: Quantitative: too little of a normal chain
Gene deletions in most α-thalassemias; point mutations affecting transcription, splicing or translation in most β-thalassemias
Amino acid substitution, deletion or elongation
Unpaired chains precipitate and damage the membrane: early death in the marrow or rapid removal from the circulation
Abnormal solubility (sickle cell), unstable hemoglobin, or altered oxygen affinity

ul: The two overlap: some hemoglobinopathies also reduce chain output and so are thalassemias too, but most are not.

items.p: A 19-year-old with lifelong hemolysis has a crisis the night after a hot hike at 2,000 m with little water. Hb 8.2 g/dL, high reticulocytes and LDH, unconjugated bilirubin. Electrophoresis: no HbA, about 90% HbS, 8% HbF, 2% HbA2 — homozygous HbSS.

ul: The mutation: each β chain carries glutamate to valine at position 6. Losing glutamate's negative charge is why HbS runs differently on the gel, and valine is hydrophobic sitting on a surface that should be hydrophilic.

The switch: in the T state a hydrophobic pocket on the β chain is exposed; the valine of one HbS slots into that pocket on a neighbour and the molecules stack into long rigid fibers. In the R state the pocket is hidden and oxygenated HbS stays soluble. Fibers therefore form wherever oxygen is released.
The cells become stiff and sticky: they block small vessels (ischemic pain) and are destroyed early (hemolysis, jaundice).

table: Higher temperature, CO2 and H+: right shift
HbS more concentrated, fibers form much faster

ul: Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Carriers (HbAS) have about 40% HbS, usually no symptoms, and some protection against severe malaria.
HbF protects because γ chains do not join the fibers, so babies are well until HbF falls; hydroxyurea raises HbF to prevent crises.

Crisis treatment: pain relief, IV fluids, warmth, oxygen if the saturation is low, and treat any infection. Bone marrow transplant can be curative, and the CRISPR gene therapy approved in 2023 reactivates HbF in the patient's own stem cells.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old has had pale skin, yellow sclerae and episodes of bone pain since childhood, and a crisis follows a hot high-altitude hike with little water. Which property of his hemoglobin explains this?

options.B: It is produced in reduced amounts
options.C: It holds oxygen too tightly to release it
options.D: It unfolds and precipitates when oxidized
options.E: It carries iron permanently in the ferric state

questions.explanation: Lifelong hemolysis with pain crises triggered by altitude, heat and dehydration points to HbS, which stacks into rigid fibers whenever it gives up oxygen. B: That is a thalassemia, which does not polymerize. C: An altered-affinity variant. D: An unstable hemoglobin. E: Methemoglobinemia.

questions.stem: What signals the kidney to release erythropoietin?

options.A: A fall in the plasma iron level
options.D: A fall in the blood pH

questions.explanation: Decreased oxygen in the tissues signals the kidney to release erythropoietin, which stimulates the production of red cells. A: Iron status does not trigger release. B: A product of heme breakdown. D: Not the stimulus described. E: An intracellular effector.

questions.stem: A patient oozes from small cuts for far longer than normal although his clotting factor levels are normal. Which blood cell type is at fault?
questions.explanation: The blood cells are erythrocytes, leukocytes and thrombocytes; the thrombocytes (platelets) function in blood clotting. A: Oxygen transport. B: Defense against infection. C: Immature red cells. E: The marrow precursors of all three.

questions.stem: How thick is a typical red cell?
questions.explanation: A typical red cell is a flexible biconcave disk with a diameter of 6–8 microns and a thickness of 2 microns. A: Thinner than described. B: Thicker than described. C: That is the lower end of the diameter. D: That is the upper end of the diameter.

questions.stem: Besides transporting oxygen, which function do red cells perform?

options.B: Buffering the blood by binding protons

questions.explanation: Red cells transport oxygen, buffer the blood by binding protons (which also allows CO2 to be carried as bicarbonate), and do both because of hemoglobin. A: The kidney does this. C: The liver does this. D: Leukocytes do this. E: The liver does this.

questions.stem: A red cell cannot switch to fatty acids when glucose runs short. Why not?

options.B: Its hemoglobin consumes the oxygen it carries
options.C: Its lifespan is too short for enzymes to work
options.D: It cannot maintain a membrane potential

questions.explanation: The red cell has limited metabolic function owing to its lack of internal organelles, so glycolysis is the main energy-generating pathway. A: Glucose entry is intact. B: Hemoglobin carries oxygen rather than using it. C: Enzymes function throughout its life. D: Not the reason given.

questions.stem: Red cells incubated with glucose release lactate steadily. What does converting pyruvate to lactate achieve?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis is the main energy-generating pathway, with lactate production regenerating NAD+ so that glycolysis can continue. A: Comes from the hexose monophosphate shunt. B: Comes from the Rapoport-Luebering shunt. D: Uses NADH that glycolysis has made. E: The red cell has none.

questions.stem: A man is given a drug that oxidizes the iron of his hemoglobin. Which form of hemoglobin results?
questions.explanation: Methemoglobin is the ferric (Fe3+) form of hemoglobin. A: Hemoglobin with oxygen bound. B: The unbound form. C: Hemoglobin with CO2 at the N terminus. E: Hemoglobin with carbon monoxide bound.

questions.stem: Which glycolytic product reduces methemoglobin back to the ferrous state?
questions.explanation: The NADH produced in glycolysis is used to reduce the ferric form of hemoglobin, methemoglobin, to the normal ferrous state. A: From the hexose monophosphate shunt, used to regenerate glutathione. C: The energy currency of glycolysis. D: The end product of anaerobic glycolysis. E: An allosteric effector of oxygen binding.

questions.stem: Which pathway produces 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis branches into a side pathway, the Rapoport-Luebering shunt, in which 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate is produced. B: Generates NADPH. C: Needs mitochondria. D: Handles oxidative stress. E: Recycles lactate in the liver.

questions.stem: A man's red cells lyse after an oxidant drug because reduced glutathione cannot be replenished. Which pathway has failed?
questions.explanation: The hexose monophosphate shunt generates NADPH, which protects red cell membrane lipids and proteins from oxidation through regeneration of reduced glutathione. A: Supplies energy and NADH. C: Makes 2,3-BPG. D: Needs mitochondria. E: A hepatic pathway.

questions.stem: About how many hemoglobin molecules does one red cell contain?
questions.explanation: There are around 270 million hemoglobin molecules per red cell. A: Far fewer than described. B: Far fewer than described. C: Fewer than described. D: More than described.

questions.stem: What proportion of the oxygen in blood is carried by red cells?
questions.explanation: Red cells transport around 98% of the oxygen present in the blood. A: Understates the share. B: Understates the share. D: Understates the share. E: A small share is dissolved in plasma.

questions.stem: How does hemoglobin stay soluble at the concentration found inside a red cell?

options.A: Hydrophilic side chains lie on the surface
options.B: The heme pockets open onto the surface
options.C: Disulfide bridges link the four chains
options.D: The tetramer carries no net charge

questions.explanation: Because of the high hemoglobin concentration, solubility is helped by the distribution of side chains: hydrophobic residues sit in the interior core and hydrophilic residues on the water-exposed surface. B: Heme sits in a hydrophobic pocket. C: The chains are not linked this way. D: Not the described mechanism. E: That describes HbA1c.

questions.stem: How many heme groups does one hemoglobin molecule contain?
questions.explanation: One hemoglobin molecule has 4 heme groups (iron plus a porphyrin ring) and 4 globin chains. A: That is myoglobin. B: Fewer than in the tetramer. C: More than in the tetramer. E: More than in the tetramer.

questions.stem: A variant hemoglobin loses its heme because one residue in the pocket is replaced. Which residue normally coordinates the heme iron?
questions.explanation: Heme sits in a hydrophobic pocket with its iron coordinated to the proximal histidine, and it is not covalently linked to the globin. B: Not the coordinating residue. C: A surface charge, not a ligand. D: The CO2 binding site. E: Not the coordinating residue.

questions.stem: How is heme held in the globin chain?

options.C: By an ester link to a serine
options.D: By a pocket, with no covalent bond
options.E: By a peptide bond to the chain

questions.explanation: Heme sits in a hydrophobic pocket and is not covalently linked to the globin. A: Heme is not covalently linked here. B: Not the attachment described. C: Not the attachment described. E: Not the attachment described.

questions.stem: How many oxygen molecules can one hemoglobin tetramer transport?
questions.explanation: Each heme group reversibly binds one oxygen molecule, so the tetramer transports four. A: Each heme binds one. B: Fewer than the tetramer carries. C: More than the tetramer carries. D: More than the tetramer carries.

questions.stem: Which chromosome carries the α-globin-like genes?
questions.explanation: In adults the globin part is one pair of α-globin-like chains (chromosome 16) and one pair of β-globin-like chains (chromosome 11). A: Carries the β-globin-like genes. B: Not a globin locus here. D: Not a globin locus here. E: Not a globin locus here.

questions.stem: Which chromosome carries the β-globin-like genes?
questions.explanation: The β-globin-like gene cluster lies on chromosome 11; the α-globin-like cluster lies on chromosome 16. A: Carries the α-globin-like genes. C: Not a globin locus here. D: Not a globin locus here. E: Not a globin locus here.

questions.stem: Electrophoresis in a healthy adult shows a band making up 2–3% of total hemoglobin. Which chain composition does it have?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin A2 is α2δ2 and makes up 2–3% of total hemoglobin; HbA (α2β2) is 96–97% and HbF (α2γ2) under 1%. A: HbA, 96–97% of the total. B: HbF, under 1% in an adult. C: HbA1c. E: Not an adult hemoglobin here.

questions.stem: A newborn's hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly than his mother's does. Which hemoglobin is responsible?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin F (α2γ2) makes up under 1% of adult hemoglobin and has a higher oxygen affinity. B: The main adult hemoglobin. C: A minor adult hemoglobin. D: Glycated HbA. E: An abnormal hemoglobin.

questions.stem: A patient's HbA1c is 7.4%. What does this value reflect?

options.A: Plasma glucose over the last 24 hours
options.B: Iron stores over the last 3 months
options.C: Plasma glucose over the last 2–3 months

questions.explanation: HbA1c is glycated HbA β chains and measures plasma glucose over the last 2–3 months; a value of 6.5% or more is diagnostic for diabetes. A: A single glucose measurement does that. B: Ferritin reflects iron stores. D: Not what the test measures. E: HbF is measured separately.

questions.stem: How many amino acids are in an α-globin chain?
questions.explanation: Primary structure: α chains have 141 amino acids and non-α chains 146. A: The length of a non-α chain. C: Not the stated length. D: Not the stated length. E: Not the stated length.

questions.stem: Which level of globin structure describes the tetramer of two heterodimers?
questions.explanation: Quaternary structure is the tetramer of two heterodimers, with allosteric interactions between them. A: The amino acid sequence. B: Helical segments joined by loops. C: Globular folding of one subunit. D: Not a level of globin structure.

questions.stem: Which diffusible ligand does hemoglobin carry to help control vascular tone?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin interacts with three diffusible ligands: O2 for delivery, CO2 for elimination and NO for control of vascular tone. A: Carried for elimination by the lungs. B: Carried for delivery to tissues. D: A poison, not a physiological ligand. E: Leaves the red cell to buffer the blood.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin shuttles oxygen all day without its heme carrier being oxidized. In which state does the iron stay?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin transports O2 from the lungs to peripheral tissues without oxidation of its heme carrier: the iron remains in the ferrous state. A: Hemoglobin with ferric iron is methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen. C: Not a biological form here. D: Not a form described. E: Iron stays in the ring.

questions.stem: A pulse oximeter emits infrared light at roughly which wavelength?
questions.explanation: A pulse oximeter uses two lights: red at about 660 nm and infrared at about 940 nm. A: Not a wavelength used. B: Not a wavelength used. C: That is the red light. D: Not a wavelength used.

questions.stem: Why does venous blood look darker than arterial blood?

options.E: Venous blood has a lower hematocrit

questions.explanation: Oxygenated hemoglobin lets red light through and absorbs more infrared, so arterial blood looks bright red; deoxygenated hemoglobin absorbs more red light, so venous blood looks darker. A: Bilirubin is a plasma pigment. B: Acidity does not change the colour. C: Methemoglobin is a small fraction. E: The hematocrit is not the reason.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin reaches a pulmonary capillary and oxygen binds. What happens first to the tetramer?
questions.explanation: Binding of O2 induces changes that break the inter-dimer bonds; the dimers then rotate relative to each other and hemoglobin shifts to the R state. B: Oxidation would give methemoglobin. C: BPG binds the deoxygenated form. D: The tetramer stays intact. E: That happens in the tissues.

questions.stem: What does rotation of the two dimers on each other achieve?

options.A: It exposes the heme iron to plasma
options.B: It converts α chains into β chains

questions.explanation: The dimers rotate on each other to increase and decrease the inter-dimer distance, which facilitates the uptake and release of O2. A: Heme stays in its pocket. B: Chains are not interconverted. C: BPG stays in the cell. E: The histidine stays coordinated.

questions.stem: Which hemoglobin conformation has relatively low oxygen affinity?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin exists in two alternating conformations: T (taut) deoxygenated with relatively low O2 affinity and R (relaxed) oxygenated with high affinity. A: The oxygenated, high-affinity conformation. C: HbA1c, not a conformational state. D: CO2 bound at the N terminus. E: Methemoglobin.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin reaches the lungs, binds oxygen and its dimers rotate. Which conformation does it now hold?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin picks up O2 in the lungs; binding breaks the inter-dimer bonds, the dimers rotate and hemoglobin shifts to the R (relaxed) state with higher O2 affinity. A: The deoxygenated conformation it has just left. B: Formed when CO2 binds in the tissues. D: Methemoglobin, which carries no oxygen. E: HbA1c, unrelated to conformation.

questions.stem: A hemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid rather than a straight line. What produces its steep middle section?

options.A: 2,3-BPG is displaced from the central cavity
options.C: The heme iron changes oxidation state
options.E: The first oxygen bound speeds the rest

questions.explanation: Once the first O2 binds, binding of O2 to the remaining hemes is accelerated, which gives the steeply rising section of the sigmoid curve. A: BPG release is not the mechanism. B: A separate reaction. C: The iron stays ferrous. D: Part of the chloride shift.

questions.stem: What is the communication between the four hemes of hemoglobin called?
questions.explanation: The acceleration of O2 binding after the first heme is occupied suggests communication between the four hemes, referred to as heme-heme interaction. B: Describes a negative effector. C: The effect of H+ on affinity. D: The exchange of Cl- for bicarbonate. E: Oxygen-driven CO2 release.

questions.stem: Which ion is one of the four primary negative regulators of hemoglobin's oxygen affinity?
questions.explanation: The four primary negative regulators are CO2, H+, Cl- and 2,3-BPG. A: Not one of the four. B: Not one of the four. C: Not one of the four. D: Not one of the four.

questions.stem: A variant hemoglobin has lost the positive charges in the cleft between its β chains and binds 2,3-BPG poorly. Which site is affected?

options.A: The heme pocket of each α chain
options.B: The central cavity between the β chains
options.C: The N terminus of each globin chain
options.E: The surface valine of the β chain

questions.explanation: Between the two beta chains is the binding site for 2,3-BPG, which is synthesized through the Rapoport-Luebering shunt. A: Occupied by heme. C: The CO2 binding site. D: Not the BPG site. E: That is the HbS substitution.

questions.stem: How does 2,3-BPG change oxygen handling?

options.C: It displaces CO2 from the N terminus
options.E: It blocks chloride entry into the cell

questions.explanation: When BPG binds it stabilizes the T state, promoting delivery of O2 to the tissues; in the lungs the pO2 is high enough to force O2 loading despite BPG. A: Oxygen binding does that. B: Oxidation gives methemoglobin. C: Not its action. E: Not its action.

questions.stem: A unit of stored blood has lost most of its 2,3-BPG. What follows for its hemoglobin?
questions.explanation: When 2,3-BPG is not available, or not bound in the central cavity, hemoglobin can be converted to HbO2 more readily. A: BPG is what stabilizes the T state. B: A right shift needs more BPG, not less. D: CO2 carriage is separate. E: Oxidation is a separate process.

questions.stem: Why does fetal hemoglobin hold oxygen more tightly than HbA?

options.D: It is glycated at its β chains

questions.explanation: HbF binds 2,3-BPG weakly, so less of it is held in the low-affinity T state. B: Ferric iron carries no oxygen. C: HbF is α2γ2. D: HbF has no β chains. E: Chloride lowers affinity.

questions.stem: Blood leaving an exercising muscle carries a large CO2 load. In which form is most of it travelling?
questions.explanation: CO2 is hydrated by carbonic anhydrase to carbonic acid, then converted to H+ and bicarbonate: about 70% of the total. A: Only 5–10%. B: Only 20–25%. C: The heme site carries oxygen. D: That is the 2,3-BPG site.

questions.stem: What share of CO2 travels as carbaminohemoglobin?
questions.explanation: CO2 is transported dissolved (5–10%), as carbaminohemoglobin (20–25%) and as bicarbonate (70%). A: The dissolved fraction. C: Not a stated fraction. D: The bicarbonate fraction. E: Not a stated fraction.

questions.stem: In a tissue capillary some CO2 binds hemoglobin directly rather than becoming bicarbonate. Where does it attach?
questions.explanation: CO2 binds directly to the N terminus of globins to form carbaminohemoglobin, which stabilizes the T state. A: That site carries oxygen. B: That is the 2,3-BPG site. D: That residue holds the heme iron. E: That is the HbS substitution.

questions.stem: What effect does carbaminohemoglobin formation have on hemoglobin?
questions.explanation: CO2 binds the N terminus of globins to form carbaminohemoglobin and stabilize the T state. B: Oxygen binding does that. C: CO2 is a negative regulator. D: Oxidation gives methemoglobin. E: CO2 and BPG act at different sites.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the red cell enzyme that converts CO2 to carbonic acid. Which enzyme is blocked?
questions.explanation: CO2 is hydrated by carbonic anhydrase to H2CO3, then converted to H+ and bicarbonate. A: Makes 2,3-BPG. B: Handles peroxides. C: The first step of the HMP shunt. E: Converts pyruvate to lactate.

questions.stem: Hydration of CO2 floods the red cell with H+ yet its pH barely moves. What buffers that H+?
questions.explanation: Within red cells the H+ is buffered by hemoglobin and phosphate, while the bicarbonate is transported into the blood to buffer H+ from other metabolic acids. B: Plasma proteins, outside the cell. C: An enzyme rather than a buffer. D: Handles oxidative stress. E: Ions exchanged, not buffers.

questions.stem: Blood reaches a pulmonary capillary and unloads CO2. Which change then lets hemoglobin bind oxygen more readily?
questions.explanation: In the lungs the equilibrium reverses: hemoglobin loses some of its H+, a feature that allows it to bind oxygen more readily. A: Chloride lowers affinity. C: BPG lowers affinity. D: CO2 is released in the lungs. E: Oxidation gives methemoglobin.

questions.stem: A sprinter's working muscle is acidic. What does the H+ do to the hemoglobin passing through?
questions.explanation: H+ stabilizes the T state by stabilizing the inter-subunit bonds and 2,3-BPG binding, so more oxygen is released. A: Oxidation gives methemoglobin. B: H+ strengthens BPG binding. C: Oxygen binding does that. D: CO2 does that.

questions.stem: What is the effect of pH on hemoglobin's oxygen affinity called?
questions.explanation: The effect of H+ on hemoglobin's oxygen affinity, through stabilization of the T state, is the Bohr effect. A: Oxygen-driven release of H+ and CO2. B: Exchange of Cl- for bicarbonate. D: Cooperativity between hemes. E: The pathway making 2,3-BPG.

questions.stem: In the lungs, oxygen binding makes hemoglobin give up H+ and CO2. What is this called?
questions.explanation: When O2 binds in the lungs, hemoglobin shifts to the R state and releases H+ and CO2, helping CO2 unloading: the Haldane effect. A: The effect of H+ on oxygen affinity. B: Exchange of Cl- for bicarbonate. C: Accelerated binding of later oxygen molecules. E: The pathway making 2,3-BPG.

questions.stem: In a tissue capillary, bicarbonate pours out of the red cell. Why does chloride move in at the same time?

options.E: To carry CO2 to the lungs

questions.explanation: Diffusion of bicarbonate out of red cells in the tissues must be coupled to Cl- movement into them to maintain electrical neutrality: the chloride shift. A: The heme site carries oxygen. C: The enzyme needs no chloride here. D: Chloride stabilizes the T state. E: Bicarbonate does that.

questions.stem: How does chloride lower hemoglobin's oxygen affinity?

options.E: By acidifying the red cell cytosol

questions.explanation: Cl- lowers O2 affinity mainly by binding deoxy-Hb directly, stabilizing the T state. A: BPG binding is not displaced by chloride. B: CO2 does that. D: Oxidation gives methemoglobin. E: H+ acts separately.

questions.stem: Venous blood leaving a resting tissue has a pO2 of 40 mmHg. What is the hemoglobin saturation?
questions.explanation: 75% saturation in the peripheral tissues at a pO2 of 40 mmHg (venous blood); about 98% in the lungs at an arterial pO2 of 95 mmHg. B: Lower than the venous value. C: Lower than the venous value. D: Closer to arterial blood. E: The arterial value.

questions.stem: At what arterial pO2 is hemoglobin about 98% saturated?
questions.explanation: About 98% saturation is reached in the lungs at an arterial pO2 of 95 mmHg. A: Far below the arterial value. B: The venous value. C: Below the arterial value. D: Above the arterial value.

questions.stem: Saturation falls from about 98% in the lungs to 75% in a resting tissue. What fraction of the oxygen load has been delivered?
questions.explanation: Saturation falls from about 98% in the lungs to 75% in the tissues: 25% of the O2 load is released. A: Less than the stated fraction. B: More than the stated fraction. C: That is the venous saturation value. E: That is the arterial saturation value.

questions.stem: What does the plateau of the curve between 70 and 100 mmHg provide?

options.A: Faster release of oxygen in the tissues
options.E: A safety margin against falls in pO2

questions.explanation: The plateau between 70 and 100 mmHg pO2 constitutes a safety mechanism against variations in pO2. A: That happens on the steep part. B: The plateau does not change affinity. C: CO2 transport is separate. D: Unrelated to the plateau.

questions.stem: A patient with lung disease has an arterial pO2 of 50 mmHg instead of 100. Roughly how far does hemoglobin saturation fall?
questions.explanation: If the pO2 dropped from 100 to 50 mmHg there would only be a corresponding drop of about 15% in hemoglobin saturation. A: Understates the fall. B: Overstates the fall. D: Overstates the fall. E: Overstates the fall.

questions.stem: What does P50 express?

options.A: The pO2 at which hemoglobin is half-saturated
options.B: The pO2 of normal venous blood
options.C: The saturation reached at a pO2 of 50 mmHg
options.D: The pO2 at which the curve plateaus
options.E: The partial pressure of CO2 in the tissues

questions.explanation: P50 is an expression of hemoglobin's affinity for O2: the pO2 at which hemoglobin is half-saturated with oxygen. B: A fixed physiological value. C: Reverses the definition. D: The plateau starts around 70 mmHg. E: A different gas.

questions.stem: A patient's hemoglobin has a P50 below the normal value. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: A low P50 indicates high affinity for oxygen, with the dissociation curve shifted to the left. A: That goes with a high P50. C: That raises P50. D: That raises P50. E: That raises P50.

questions.stem: Through which part of hemoglobin do CO2 and H+ change its conformation?
questions.explanation: pH (Bohr effect) and pCO2 affect P50 because CO2 and H+ bind the globin portion of hemoglobin and alter its conformation. A: Binds oxygen itself. B: Holds the iron. C: The 2,3-BPG site. E: Anchors the heme.

questions.stem: Which change in body state lowers hemoglobin's oxygen affinity by altering its conformation?

options.D: A fall in the white cell count

questions.explanation: A high temperature alters hemoglobin's conformation and raises P50, alongside pH, pCO2 and 2,3-BPG. A: Not a regulator of affinity. B: Not a regulator of affinity. C: Not a regulator of affinity. D: Not a regulator of affinity.

questions.stem: After three weeks at 3,500 m, which red cell change improves oxygen delivery to a climber's tissues?
questions.explanation: 2,3-BPG increases in response to chronic hypoxia (high altitude, smoking, COPD), enhancing dissociation of O2 in the tissues. A: Chloride handling is unchanged. B: CO2 handling is unchanged. C: Methemoglobin carries no oxygen. E: A minor hemoglobin, not an adaptation.

questions.stem: Which group of patients would be expected to have a raised 2,3-BPG from chronic hypoxia?
questions.explanation: 2,3-BPG increases in response to chronic hypoxia: high altitude, smoking and COPD. A: Not listed as a hypoxic stimulus. C: An iron-loading disorder. D: No effect described. E: No effect described.

questions.stem: During hard exercise, muscle takes up more oxygen at an unchanged capillary pO2. Why?

options.C: The P50 falls in the muscle

questions.explanation: The more active a tissue, the greater its pCO2, H+ and temperature; at any given pO2 this makes hemoglobin release more oxygen to the active cells. B: Red cell mass does not change acutely. C: A falling P50 would hold oxygen tighter. D: CO2 handling continues. E: HbF production does not change acutely.

questions.stem: Why does erythropoietin doping raise the risk of thrombosis?

options.C: It raises the circulating red cells

questions.explanation: Erythropoietin increases the number of circulating red cells, making the blood thicker and raising thrombosis risk, while improving aerobic capacity. A: Not the described mechanism. B: Not the described mechanism. D: Not the described mechanism. E: Not the described mechanism.

questions.stem: Why do EPO-like drugs carry an FDA boxed warning in cancer patients?
questions.explanation: EPO also activates cell survival pathways through its receptor; in cancer patients, trials showed EPO-like drugs can shorten survival or speed tumor growth, hence the boxed warning since 2007. A: Not the reported harm. B: Not the reported harm. C: Not the reported harm. D: Not the reported harm.

questions.stem: A man rescued from a smoky basement is confused, and his oxygen saturation reads normal. Why is oxygen delivery to his tissues impaired?

options.A: Carbon monoxide oxidizes the heme iron
options.B: Carbon monoxide shifts the curve to the left
options.C: Carbon monoxide stabilizes the T state

questions.explanation: CO competes with O2 for the binding sites and, through conformational effects, also shifts the dissociation curve to the left, so less O2 is released to the tissues. A: It binds the oxygen site rather than oxidizing iron. C: It has the opposite conformational effect. D: CO2 handling is not the problem. E: That would aid release, not impair it.

questions.stem: How much more strongly does carbon monoxide bind hemoglobin's oxygen-binding sites than oxygen does?
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide has 200 to 250 times higher affinity for the oxygen-binding sites of hemoglobin than O2 has. A: Far below the stated figure. B: Below the stated figure. C: Above the stated figure. E: Above the stated figure.

questions.stem: Which defect defines the thalassemias?

options.A: Reduced production of a globin chain
options.B: An amino acid substitution in a globin chain
options.C: Loss of the heme binding pocket

questions.explanation: Genetic errors resulting in quantitative defects in globin chain production cause the thalassemias. B: That defines a hemoglobinopathy. C: Not the defect described. D: Methemoglobinemia. E: An affinity problem, not a thalassemia.

questions.stem: A child with β-thalassemia major has severe anemia with red cells dying in the marrow. What damages those cells?
questions.explanation: With unbalanced chain synthesis the non-paired globin chains precipitate and damage the cell membrane, causing early cell death in the marrow or rapid removal from the circulation. A: The lesion of sickle cell disease. B: Immune hemolysis. D: Immune hemolysis. E: The lesion of oxidative hemolysis.

questions.stem: Which molecular change underlies most α-thalassemias?
questions.explanation: Thalassemias usually result from underproduction of normal globin proteins, often through gene deletions (most α-thalassemias). A: The usual cause of β-thalassemia. B: The lesion of a hemoglobinopathy. C: A rarer hemoglobinopathy mutation. E: Not a described cause.

questions.stem: Most β-thalassemias result from which kind of mutation?

options.A: Deletions of the whole gene cluster
options.B: Amino acid substitutions on the surface
options.C: Point mutations in the globin gene

questions.explanation: Most β-thalassemias arise from point mutations in the globin gene affecting transcription, splicing or translation. A: The usual cause in α-thalassemia. B: The lesion of a hemoglobinopathy. D: Not a described cause. E: Not a described cause.

questions.stem: What makes a disorder a hemoglobinopathy rather than a thalassemia?

options.A: Too little of a normal chain is made
options.B: It is a qualitative defect of the chain
options.C: The heme group cannot be inserted
options.D: The red cell membrane is abnormal

questions.explanation: Hemoglobinopathies are qualitative defects of the globin chains from substitutions, deletions or elongation; thalassemias are quantitative defects of production. A: That is a thalassemia. C: Not the distinction described. D: A membrane disorder. E: Deletions reduce output, as in α-thalassemia.

questions.stem: Which functional defect does sickle cell anemia represent among the hemoglobinopathies?
questions.explanation: Abnormalities in chain structure give abnormal solubility (sickle cell anemia), unstable hemoglobin or altered oxygen affinity. A: A different functional defect. B: A different functional defect. C: That is a thalassemia. D: Not a listed defect.

questions.stem: Sequencing of a sickle cell patient's β-globin gene shows a single changed codon at position 6. Which substitution is it?
questions.explanation: Each β chain of HbS carries one substitution at position 6: glutamate to valine. B: A different variant. C: The α chain is not affected. D: A different variant. E: Not the substitution described.

questions.stem: Why does HbS move differently from HbA on electrophoresis?

options.A: Valine makes the molecule much larger
options.D: HbS is glycated at the β chains
options.E: The substitution removes a negative charge

questions.explanation: Electrophoresis separates species by charge; losing glutamate's charge is why HbS moves differently on the gel. A: The size change is negligible. B: HbS has normal α chains. C: γ chains belong to HbF. D: That describes HbA1c.

questions.stem: The HbS mutation places a valine on the outside of the molecule. Why does its position matter?

options.A: Valine cannot be reached by antibodies

questions.explanation: Valine is hydrophobic and sits on the surface of the molecule, where hydrophilic residues normally keep hemoglobin soluble. A: Immunity is not involved. B: Heme binding is normal. C: The BPG site is unchanged. E: The chains still pair.

questions.stem: Why do HbS fibers form only when oxygen has been released?

options.A: The valine is buried in the T state
options.B: A hydrophobic pocket is exposed in the T state
options.C: The heme iron is oxidized in the tissues

questions.explanation: In deoxyhemoglobin a hydrophobic pocket on the β chain becomes exposed; the valine of one HbS fits into that pocket on a neighbouring deoxy-HbS and the molecules stack into long rigid fibers. A: The T state exposes the pocket. C: The iron stays ferrous. D: BPG binds the deoxygenated form. E: Chloride does not drive polymerization.

questions.stem: What happens to HbS when it is fully oxygenated?
questions.explanation: In the R state the hydrophobic pocket is hidden, so oxygenated HbS stays soluble. A: Fibers form in the deoxygenated state. B: That is oxidative damage. D: Hemoglobins are not interconverted. E: Heme stays bound.

questions.stem: Why do sickled cells cause both ischemic pain and jaundice?

options.C: They are too small to carry oxygen
options.D: They activate the coagulation cascade directly

questions.explanation: Bent and distorted cells are stiff and sticky: they block small vessels (ischemic pain) and are destroyed early (hemolysis, jaundice). B: Bilirubin comes from their breakdown. C: Size is not the problem. D: Not the described mechanism. E: That is hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.stem: Electrophoresis in a 19-year-old shows no HbA, about 90% HbS, 8% HbF and 2% HbA2. Which condition is this?
questions.explanation: No HbA with about 90% HbS means both β-globin genes carry the sickle mutation: HbSS. A: Would show HbA as well. B: Would show mostly HbA with a raised HbA2. D: Would show a much higher HbF and no HbS. E: Would be mostly HbA.

questions.stem: About what share of hemoglobin is HbS in a person with sickle cell trait?
questions.explanation: Carriers (sickle cell trait, HbAS) have about 40% HbS, usually with no symptoms. B: Below the carrier level. C: Below the carrier level. D: Above the carrier level. E: The level in homozygous disease.

questions.stem: Which advantage do sickle cell carriers have?
questions.explanation: Carriers usually have no symptoms and some protection against severe malaria. A: Not an effect of the trait. B: The trait does not change affinity. C: Not an effect of the trait. E: Not an effect of the trait.

questions.stem: Why does a high fetal hemoglobin level protect a child with sickle cell disease?

options.B: HbF carries its iron in the ferric state
options.C: HbF dissolves the fibers already formed
options.D: HbF blocks the valine from being made
options.E: γ chains do not join the fibers

questions.explanation: HbF protects because γ chains replace β chains and do not join the fibers, so babies are well until HbF falls. A: HbF binds BPG weakly. B: Ferric iron carries no oxygen. C: It prevents rather than dissolves. D: The mutation is unchanged.

questions.stem: A child with four crises a year is started on a drug that raises his fetal hemoglobin. Which drug is it?
questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea raises HbF to prevent crises. A: An iron chelator. C: Supports erythropoiesis. D: A corticosteroid. E: Raises the red cell count.

questions.stem: A patient in a painful sickle crisis has an oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. Which measure belongs in his initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Treatment of a crisis is pain relief, IV fluids, warmth, oxygen if the saturation is low, and treatment of any infection. A: Oxygen is given when the saturation is low. B: Not listed for a routine crisis. C: Prevents crises rather than treating one. D: Treats iron overload.

questions.stem: Which treatment can cure sickle cell disease?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow transplant can be curative, and CRISPR gene therapy approved in 2023 reactivates HbF in the patient's stem cells. A: Reduces crises without curing. B: A temporary measure. C: Supports erythropoiesis. E: Removes excess iron.

questions.stem: Why does dehydration make a sickle crisis worse?
questions.explanation: Dehydration shrinks the red cells; HbS is more concentrated and fibers form much faster. A: Acidosis, not alkalosis, promotes sickling. C: Heat, not cold, was the trigger here. D: A fall would hold oxygen tighter. E: A right shift, not a left shift, is the issue.

questions.stem: Chronic anemia in sickle cell disease raises the 2,3-BPG level. What does this do to oxygen handling?

options.C: It shifts the curve to the right

questions.explanation: Chronic anemia raises 2,3-BPG and shifts the curve right: better O2 delivery, but more deoxy-HbS and so more fiber formation. A: BPG stabilizes the T state. B: BPG does not change HbF. D: CO2 carriage is unaffected. E: Chloride handling is unaffected.

questions.stem: Which feature belongs to β-thalassemia major rather than to sickle cell disease?

options.A: Too few β chains are made
options.B: One amino acid substitution in the β chain
options.C: Polymerization of hemoglobin in the T state
options.D: Pain crises from occluded small vessels
options.E: A hydrophobic residue on the molecule's surface

questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease is a qualitative defect (an abnormal β chain); β-thalassemia major is quantitative (too few β chains from many different mutations). B: The sickle lesion. C: The sickle lesion. D: The sickle presentation. E: The sickle lesion.
